**The Weight of a Single Leaf**

I remember the first time I noticed how much a single leaf weighed. It was in the autumn of my childhood, when the trees outside my window turned from green to gold. I picked one up—just one—between my thumb and forefinger, and for a moment, I held it in the palm of my hand, feeling its delicate curve, the way it trembled in the breeze.

Then I let it go.

It didn’t fall fast. It drifted down, slow and deliberate, as if it were testing the air. I watched it until it landed on the grass, where it lay still, a tiny, perfect thing. I wondered if it knew it was going to die. If it felt the weight of its own existence, the way it would soon be nothing but dust and memory.

That’s the thing about leaves—they’re so fragile, yet they carry the entire story of the tree. They don’t just fall; they *choose* to. They let go of the branch, of the sun, of the wind, and they trust that the earth will hold them.

I thought about that a lot as I grew older. About how we, too, are made of fragile things—memories, regrets, the weight of our own stories. We hold them in our hands, sometimes too tightly, sometimes too lightly, and then we let go. Some things fall gently, some with a thud, and some never land at all.

But the leaf, in its quiet way, taught me something. That even the smallest thing can carry the weight of the world. That sometimes, the best we can do is let go—and trust that the earth will hold us too.

And so, I let the leaf go.
